I personally preferred the basic topological and confidence interval visualizations because they were relatively intuitive and easier to interpret.

In my EEG research experience, topoplots are commonly useful at two stages: first, during data quality assessment and artifact identification, and second, when interpreting the spatial distribution of neural activity or ERP amplitudes.

I found the uncertainty markers visually distracting, as they increased perceptual clutter and diverted attention from the underlying signal. Similarly, the bivariate color maps were cognitively demanding because multiple color variations made it difficult to distinguish signal magnitude from uncertainty.

I believe adjacent plots showing the signal and its uncertainty separately could be a more effective approach. They allow researchers to compare both dimensions without overloading a single visualization.

My suggestion would be to evaluate these approaches not only in terms of interpretation accuracy and response time but also perceived cognitive workload, visual search efficiency, and user preference.
